Back to the exploratory data analysis; the code is in the repository on GitHub.

Does the win-back playbook give its deeper discount where a discount euro keeps the most contribution? Not at its current rates. At the playbook's rates (15% for At Risk, 20% for Hibernating), each euro of discount retains 1.85 times as much contribution in At Risk as in Hibernating. Most of that gap comes from the deeper discount Hibernating gets: with either rate applied to both segments, At Risk retains about 1.2 times as much. A pilot against randomised holdouts tests Hibernating at both rates; if the budget is short, At Risk goes first only if At Risk retains more on an incremental basis.

The playbook gives the deeper discount to the thinner margin: after its offer At Risk keeps 37 points of order value, Hibernating 27

Realised gross margin before the playbook's win-back discount and contribution after it, in points of order value; the discount rate is the dim_Segment[Discount Approach] label. Order value is already net of each order's realised discount, which the mean realised discount averages, so the gross margin is measured after it; the win-back discount would come on top, as a further percentage off that order value.

At the playbook's rates, each 1,000 EUR of discount retains 2,465 EUR of contribution in At Risk, against 1,335 EUR in Hibernating

Contribution per 1,000 EUR of discount at the playbook's rates: (gross margin - discount rate) / discount rate x 1,000 EUR. At these rates At Risk retains 1.85 times as much per euro of discount as Hibernating; with either rate applied to both segments, about 1.2 times as much.
